Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Amanda, 19-year-old woman, presents with classic features of acute lower urinary tract infection: dysuria, urinary frequency, suprapubic aching pain (worse on urination), and new pinkish urine (likely hematuria); duration just under one week.
- No fevers, no nausea/vomiting, no back/flank pain (no evidence of upper UTI/pyelonephritis). No abnormal vaginal discharge. Stable IBS.
- Working diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (urinary tract infection), supported by transcript and DDx.
- Alternative consideration: Urethritis (STI-related, e.g., chlamydia/gonorrhea) due to unprotected sex, but less likely as no abnormal discharge or urethral-dominant pain; cystitis more consistent.
- Other differentials (low likelihood): Nephrolithiasis (no colicky/loin-to-groin pain or systemic features), drug-induced cystitis (recent cannabis use, but not a known cause).
- Planned management: Empiric antibiotics (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim), analgesia (paracetamol), enhanced fluid intake, urine sample collection for urinalysis and culture. Safety net advice given for return if worsened symptoms (fever, vomiting, back pain).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute uncomplicated cystitis (urinary tract infection): High likelihood. Classic presentation of dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, and pink urine in a young woman; no systemic symptoms or red flags.
- Urethritis (sexually transmitted infection, e.g., chlamydia/gonorrhea): Medium likelihood. Could explain symptoms given history of unprotected sex, but absence of abnormal discharge and more prominent bladder symptoms make this less likely.
- Nephrolithiasis (distal ureteral stone): Low likelihood. Pink urine and urinary frequency noted; however, lack of severe pain, back/flank tenderness, or GI upset makes this diagnosis unlikely.
